content: The tobacco industry claims that their marketing efforts are not aimed at young nonsmokers. However, evidence strongly suggests that tobacco advertising and promotional activities influence the attitudes of nonsmoking adolescents, making them more inclined to experiment with smoking. The objective of this research was to evaluate the impact of tobacco advertising and promotion on the future smoking behaviors of nonsmoking adolescents. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Tobacco Group specialized register, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, MEDLINE, the Cochrane Library, Sociological Abstracts, PsycLIT, ERIC, WorldCat, Dissertation Abstracts, ABI Inform, and Current Contents, with the search extending up to August 2011. The inclusion criteria focused on longitudinal studies that examined the smoking behaviors of individuals and their exposure to tobacco advertising, receptivity to such advertising, or brand awareness at the start of the study. These studies also assessed smoking behaviors during follow-up periods. Participants were adolescents aged 18 years or younger who were not regular smokers at the beginning of the study. The data collection process involved an initial prescreening of studies for relevance by one reviewer, followed by an independent assessment of the selected studies by two reviewers. Data extraction was performed by one reviewer and subsequently verified by a second reviewer. A total of 19 longitudinal studies, encompassing over 29,000 nonsmoking adolescents at baseline, met the inclusion criteria. These studies employed various methods to measure exposure or receptivity to tobacco advertising and promotion. For instance, some studies assessed whether participants had a favorite tobacco advertisement or used an index of receptivity based on their awareness of advertising and ownership of promotional items. One study specifically measured the number of tobacco advertisements in magazines read by participants. All studies evaluated changes in smoking behavior among participants who reported not smoking at the start of the study. In 18 out of the 19 studies, nonsmoking adolescents who demonstrated greater awareness of or receptivity to tobacco advertising were more likely to experiment with cigarettes or become smokers during the follow-up period. While the strength of the association varied across studies, and some studies controlled for potential confounding factors to differing extents, the overall trend was consistent. The authors concluded that longitudinal studies consistently indicate a strong association between exposure to tobacco advertising and promotion and the likelihood of adolescents initiating smoking. This conclusion is supported by the strength and specificity of the observed association, evidence of a dose-response relationship, the consistency of findings across numerous observational studies, the temporal relationship between exposure and subsequent smoking behaviors, and the theoretical plausibility of advertising's influence. Collectively, these findings provide robust evidence that tobacco advertising and promotion increase the probability that adolescents will begin smoking.
